extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political history and theory; scholars of Florentine/early-modern constitutional thought
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted principles and institutional criteria for forming and preserving republican governments (managing factions, structuring magistracies, deciding deliberative bodies), drawn from historical discussion of Florence (Machiavelli, Guicchiardini, Soderini, Vespuci).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution must account for human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution formed upon the nature of man, and providing against his discontented temper; instead of trusting to what is not in him (his moderation and contentment in power) may preserve union, harmony, and tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the presumed moderation or contentment of rulers or citizens. Design institutions that anticipate and check natural passions and discontent so as to preserve union and public tranquillity; such institutional design can preserve union better than despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers and bicameral legislature
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide against factions by distinct and independent legislative, executive, and judicial powers, and by two councils in the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate and make independent the executive, legislative, and judicial functions; include multiple legislative councils (two councils) to check factionalism and to manage competition within the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent and manage factions
rubrics_metrics.description: It ought to be the chief care to provide against [differences and divisions] growing up into factions; differences and divisions are for the most part prejudicial but some are of service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that divisions are inevitable; the constitution should prevent their escalation into destructive parties by institutional checks (separation of powers, bicameralism, representation) while allowing benign competition that benefits the commonwealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the three natural orders
rubrics_metrics.description: When the three natural orders in society, the high, the middle, and the low, are all represented in the government, and constitutionally placed to watch each other, emulation takes place for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representation to include distinct social orders (or their functional equivalents) so that each watches and restrains the others; this mutual oversight channels competition into public benefit rather than private factional gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of popularity matter
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two roads to popularity: public stations (gaining signal victory, prudent discharge of embassy, wise advice in council) and private life (beneficence, screening from magistrates, supplying money, promoting to honours, entertaining, distributing largesses). Popularity obtained by private means is dangerous; reputation acquired by public service conduces to the good of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage or limit private patronage, largess, and buying of followers; encourage attainment of reputation through public virtue and service to produce beneficial leaders rather than private clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magistracies distributed by a universal council
rubrics_metrics.description: All the magistrates and officers, both in the city and all its dominions, shall be distributed, from time to time, by a universal council of all those who are qualified for participation in government; without the approbation of which council new laws cannot be deliberated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a broadly representative (universal) council to allocate offices so that distribution depends on virtues and merits rather than private conspiracies or factional caprice; this prevents exclusion and opens paths to honours through public and private good conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Important deliberations handled by a selected experienced council
rubrics_metrics.description: All the most important deliberations, as those of peace and war, the examination of new laws, and generally all those things necessary to administration, shall be treated by magistrates, particularly destined to this service, in a select council of the most experienced and prudent citizens, deputed by the popular council.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex, urgent, or secret matters require a smaller, expert deliberative body (deputed by the people) to secure celerity, secrecy, and qualified judgment; avoid handling such matters in large unwieldy assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure liberty by universal consent for magistracies and laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty remains secure at all times when the distribution of magistracies, and the deliberations on new laws, depend on universal consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure key institutional decisions (appointments, foundational laws) require broad/collective approval so that no private group or intrigue can unilaterally alter the government; tie legitimacy to wide consent to maintain durable liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of authority; balance executive, senate, and people
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither concentrating all authority in the people nor in the senate alone will secure peace; without admitting both the senate and the people to a share of power, and repairing the executive from both, there can be no peace nor harmony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct balanced institutions where executive authority is distinct from and checked by both representative bodies (popular and senatorial/aristocratic) to prevent domination by any single center and to foster stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit popular government due to risks of ignorance and ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: A multitude, immersed in ignorance and involved in confusion, cannot be expected to produce prudent deliberations; applause of virtue and merit, if left to the multitude, will be confounded and may bestow most power on the most ignorant (opinions must be numbered not weighed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the dangers of pure popular rule (rewarding the ignorant, confounding gradations, fostering licentiousness). Implement institutional safeguards (selection of experienced magistrates, limits on popular competence in complex affairs) to prevent the majority from unintentionally undermining good governance.
